chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Talisi, from Abu Yahya Zakariya al-Mawsili, who said:

I asked the Imam (peace be upon him) about a man who stood at the Station (of Arafat) and news of his father's death, or the death of one of his children, reached him before he remembered God with anything or supplicated, so he became occupied with anxiety and weeping to the exclusion of supplication. Then the people departed, and he said: 'I do not see any blame upon him, but he has done poorly; let him seek forgiveness from God. Would that he had been patient and sought reward, then he would have departed from the Station with the good deeds of all the people of the Station, without any of their good deeds being diminished.'
And it is recommended that a person should frequently supplicate for his believing brothers and prefer them over himself in this regard, as narrated.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling and spiritual consequence for a pilgrer at Arafat who receives news of a death and becomes distracted by grief before supplicating?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the legal ruling of exemption from sin and the spiritual opportunity missed by a pilgrer at Arafat who is overwhelmed by grief upon hearing of a relative's death. He highlights the unique metaphysical status of the standing at Arafat, where patience (*sabr*) and counting the event as an act of worship (*ihtisab*) allow one to share in the collective good deeds of all other pilgrims, a concept reflecting the Shia emphasis on the interconnectedness of the faithful's merits. The narration concludes by linking this personal spiritual elevation to the broader ethical imperative of preferring others over oneself (*ithar*) in supplication.
